## What you will do

Albert now has a partner, a rabbit, and the rabbit's mood gets into Albert's rule for change:

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}\eta_1\\ \eta_2\end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix}A_1 & A_{cross_{12}}\\ A_{cross_{21}} & A_2\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\eta_1\\ \eta_2\end{pmatrix} +
\begin{pmatrix}B_1\\ B_2\end{pmatrix}
$$

with $\eta_1$ = Albert and $\eta_2$ = the rabbit (Exercise 1 leaves out the noise; Exercise 2 adds it). We use $A_1 = -0.6$, $A_2 = -0.4$, $A_{cross_{12}} = 1$ and $A_{cross_{21}} = 0$. Both rest at affect 5. Time is in days.

There are two exercises and a bonus question. When an exercise says **Predict first**, write down or sketch your prediction *before* running the code.

**Run this chunk first.** It contains the simulation: the same small-step method we've been using so far, now with two states that are updated together. The only thing you need to change in this sheet is the measurement interval `Dt` in Exercise 2.

```{r simulation}
times <- seq(from = 0, to = 20, by = 0.1) #time points (days)
Nsteps <- 10 #number of small steps between two time points
A1 <- -0.6 #Albert's own pull
A2 <- -0.4 #the rabbit's own pull
A12 <- 1 #effect of the rabbit on Albert (A_cross12)
A21 <- 0 #effect of Albert on the rabbit (A_cross21)
rest <- c(5, 5) #resting levels of Albert and the rabbit

simulateCouple <- function(startAlbert, startRabbit){
  B1 <- -(A1*rest[1] + A12*rest[2]) #intercepts chosen so that both rest at 'rest'
  B2 <- -(A21*rest[1] + A2*rest[2])
  Nobs <- length(times)
  Albert <- Rabbit <- rep(NA, Nobs)
  Albert[1] <- startAlbert; Rabbit[1] <- startRabbit
  for(i in 2:Nobs){
    AlbertState <- Albert[i-1]; RabbitState <- Rabbit[i-1]
    dt <- (times[i] - times[i-1]) / Nsteps
    for(stepi in 1:Nsteps){
      dAlbert <- A1*AlbertState + A12*RabbitState + B1 #Albert's slope (row 1 of the matrix)
      dRabbit <- A21*AlbertState + A2*RabbitState + B2 #the rabbit's slope (row 2 of the matrix)
      AlbertState <- AlbertState + dAlbert * dt
      RabbitState <- RabbitState + dRabbit * dt
    }
    Albert[i] <- AlbertState; Rabbit[i] <- RabbitState
  }
  data.frame(Time = times, Albert = Albert, Rabbit = Rabbit)
}

plotCouple <- function(sim){ #plot Albert and the rabbit in one figure
  long <- rbind(data.frame(Time = sim$Time, Affect = sim$Albert, Who = "Albert"),
                data.frame(Time = sim$Time, Affect = sim$Rabbit, Who = "Rabbit"))
  ggplot(long, aes(x = Time, y = Affect, colour = Who)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = rest, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Albert = "#2a78d6", Rabbit = "#7a4fb5")) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
    labs(x = "Time (days)", y = "Affect", colour = NULL)
}
```

## Exercise 1: Two bad days

A "bad day" means that someone starts at affect 1 instead of 5.

a. **Predict first:** sketch Albert and the rabbit over 20 days when (i) the rabbit has a bad day, and (ii) Albert has a bad day.

b. Run the code and compare with your sketches.

c. Which entry of the matrix makes (i) and (ii) look so different?

```{r ex-1, eval = SOLN}
plotCouple(simulateCouple(startAlbert = 5, startRabbit = 1)) + ggtitle("(i) the rabbit has a bad day")
plotCouple(simulateCouple(startAlbert = 1, startRabbit = 5)) + ggtitle("(ii) Albert has a bad day")
```

## Exercise 2: How often you measure

Many studies measure a couple's affect using some $\Delta t$ (every few hours, every day, every week) and then run a **cross-lagged regression**: Albert at the *next* measurement, predicted from Albert and the rabbit at *this* measurement:

$$\text{AlbertNext} = c + a_{11}\,\text{AlbertNow} + a_{12}\,\text{RabbitNow}$$

The coefficient $a_{12}$ of RabbitNow is the **cross-lagged effect** of the rabbit on Albert. We will do exactly what such a study does.

First run the chunk below. It simulates Albert's and the rabbit's moods over a very long time, with random kicks as in Lecture 6. Think of it as their real life, which no study ever sees completely.

```{r ex-2-life, eval = SOLN}
G1 <- 0.4; G2 <- 1.2 #size of the random kicks: Albert small, rabbit large
dtSim <- 0.025 #tiny step (days)
lifeDays <- 40000 #a very long life, so the regression results are precise
nSim <- lifeDays / dtSim
B1 <- -(A1*rest[1] + A12*rest[2]); B2 <- -(A21*rest[1] + A2*rest[2]) #both rest at 5
set.seed(606)
kick1 <- rnorm(nSim); kick2 <- rnorm(nSim) #all random kicks, drawn in advance
lifeAlbert <- lifeRabbit <- rep(5, nSim + 1)
for (k in 1:nSim) {
  dAlbert <- A1*lifeAlbert[k] + A12*lifeRabbit[k] + B1 #same rule as before ...
  dRabbit <- A21*lifeAlbert[k] + A2*lifeRabbit[k] + B2
  lifeAlbert[k+1] <- lifeAlbert[k] + dAlbert*dtSim + G1*sqrt(dtSim)*kick1[k] #... plus a random kick
  lifeRabbit[k+1] <- lifeRabbit[k] + dRabbit*dtSim + G2*sqrt(dtSim)*kick2[k]
}
```

Now the study. The chunk below measures both every `Dt` days, puts each measurement next to Albert's next measurement, and runs the regression.

a. **Predict first:** the coupling in the model is $A_{cross_{12}} = 1$. Will the regression find the same cross-lagged effect whether you measure every 3 hours, every day or every week?

b. Run the chunk with `Dt <- 1`, then change it to `0.125` (every 3 hours) and `7` (once a week). Write down the coefficient of `RabbitNow` each time.

```{r ex-2-study, eval = SOLN}
Dt <- 2 #measurement interval (days): try 1, 0.125 and 7

measured <- seq(from = 1, to = nSim + 1, by = round(Dt / dtSim)) #which moments the study sees
Albert <- lifeAlbert[measured]
Rabbit <- lifeRabbit[measured]
N <- length(Albert)

study <- data.frame(AlbertNow  = Albert[-N], #each row: this measurement ...
                    RabbitNow  = Rabbit[-N],
                    AlbertNext = Albert[-1]) #... and Albert at the next measurement
head(round(study, 2))

fit <- lm(AlbertNext ~ AlbertNow + RabbitNow, data = study)
round(coef(fit), 2) #RabbitNow = the cross-lagged effect
```

c. The chunk below repeats the same study for many intervals, from 3 hours to 2 weeks, and plots the cross-lagged effect for each. At which interval is it largest?

d. Three groups study this couple: group A every 3 hours, group B daily, group C weekly. Group C writes "the rabbit hardly affects Albert", group B writes "the rabbit strongly affects Albert". Who is right?

```{r ex-2-curve, eval = SOLN}
intervals <- c(0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 14) #measurement intervals (days)
crossLagged <- rep(NA, length(intervals))
for (i in seq_along(intervals)) { #the same study as above, once for every interval
  measured <- seq(from = 1, to = nSim + 1, by = round(intervals[i] / dtSim))
  Albert <- lifeAlbert[measured]
  Rabbit <- lifeRabbit[measured]
  N <- length(Albert)
  study <- data.frame(AlbertNow = Albert[-N], RabbitNow = Rabbit[-N], AlbertNext = Albert[-1])
  crossLagged[i] <- coef(lm(AlbertNext ~ AlbertNow + RabbitNow, data = study))["RabbitNow"]
}

ggplot(data.frame(interval = intervals, crossLagged = crossLagged), aes(x = interval, y = crossLagged)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  labs(x = "measurement interval (days)", y = "cross-lagged effect (RabbitNow)")
```

## Bonus: Design the cheapest study

Measurements cost money and participants' patience. Suppose you can afford **12 measurements** per couple, and you want to find out whether the rabbit affects Albert. You are free to choose how far apart the 12 measurements are.

The chunk below runs many such small studies for each interval: it measures the simulated life every `Dt` days, cuts it into separate studies of 12 measurements, runs the same cross-lagged regression in each study, and counts how often the `RabbitNow` coefficient is significant ($p < .05$). That proportion is the **power** of the design.

a. **Predict first:** at which interval will a 12-measurement study find the rabbit's effect most often? At 2 days, where the cross-lagged effect is largest?

b. Run the chunk. Which interval has the highest power?

c. Why is the best interval not the one with the largest cross-lagged effect? *Hint:* besides the rabbit's push, what else happens to Albert between two measurements, and what happens to that when the interval gets longer?

```{r bonus, eval = SOLN}
Nbudget <- 12 #measurements per study
intervals <- c(0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 7) #measurement intervals (days)
power <- rep(NA, length(intervals))
for (i in seq_along(intervals)) {
  measured <- seq(from = 1, to = nSim + 1, by = round(intervals[i] / dtSim)) #measure the whole life every Dt ...
  Albert <- lifeAlbert[measured]
  Rabbit <- lifeRabbit[measured]
  nStudies <- min(400, floor(length(Albert) / Nbudget)) #... and cut it into separate studies of 12 measurements
  found <- rep(NA, nStudies)
  for (s in 1:nStudies) {
    rows <- ((s - 1) * Nbudget + 1):(s * Nbudget) #the 12 measurements of study s
    a <- Albert[rows]; r <- Rabbit[rows]
    study <- data.frame(AlbertNow = a[-Nbudget], RabbitNow = r[-Nbudget], AlbertNext = a[-1])
    pValue <- summary(lm(AlbertNext ~ AlbertNow + RabbitNow, data = study))$coefficients["RabbitNow", "Pr(>|t|)"]
    found[s] <- pValue < 0.05 #did this study find the effect?
  }
  power[i] <- mean(found) #proportion of studies that found it
}

ggplot(data.frame(interval = intervals, power = power), aes(x = interval, y = power)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#eb6834") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#eb6834") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = intervals, labels = c("3h", "6h", "12h", "1d", "2d", "4d", "1w")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  labs(x = "measurement interval (log scale)", y = "power (12 measurements)")
```
